questions.q: Why should the final layer of an MLP used for classification output raw logits rather than, say, softmax-normalized probabilities?
options: Raw logits train faster on GPU
nn.CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits and internally applies log-softmax itself; pre-applying softmax would double the transformation and corrupt the gradients
PyTorch does not support applying softmax inside a model
Raw logits are required for nn.Linear to function at all
questions.explain: As covered in Lesson 10, nn.CrossEntropyLoss performs its own internal log-softmax, so the model's output layer should be a plain linear layer producing unnormalized logits.

questions.q: In the MLP training loop, which lesson's concept does `x_batch, y_batch = x_batch.to(device), y_batch.to(device)` rely on?
options: Lesson 3 (Devices), moving every batch to the same device as the model
Lesson 6 (Saving & Loading Models)
Lesson 9 (Linear Layers & Activation Functions)
Lesson 2 (Autograd)
questions.explain: Moving each batch to the same device as the model, inside the loop, is the device-agnostic pattern introduced in Lesson 3 -- it prevents the 'tensors on different devices' RuntimeError.

questions.q: What is the purpose of calling logits.argmax(dim=1) during evaluation?
options: To normalize the logits into probabilities
To select, for each example, the index of the class with the highest score, which is the model's predicted class label
To compute the loss for that batch
To reset the model's parameters
questions.explain: argmax(dim=1) returns the index of the maximum value along the class dimension for each example in the batch, giving the predicted class index that can be compared directly against integer ground-truth labels.

questions.q: During the evaluation loop, both model.eval() and torch.no_grad() are used. What distinct roles do they play?
options: They are redundant; either one alone is sufficient
model.eval() changes certain layers' behavior (e.g. dropout, batch norm) to inference mode, while torch.no_grad() separately disables gradient/graph tracking to save memory and compute
model.eval() disables gradients; torch.no_grad() switches layer behavior
Both only affect which device the model runs on
questions.explain: These two serve different purposes: eval() toggles behavior in layers that act differently during training vs. inference, while no_grad() is purely about skipping computational graph construction since gradients aren't needed for evaluation.

questions.q: In the MLP code, what does model.train() accomplish before the training loop begins?
options: It immediately runs one epoch of training
It sets the model into training mode, which matters once layers like dropout or batch norm (introduced in Chapter 3) are present, since they behave differently in train vs. eval mode
It loads a previously saved checkpoint
It freezes all the model's parameters
questions.explain: model.train() is the counterpart to model.eval(): it puts layers with mode-dependent behavior (like Dropout or BatchNorm) into their training behavior. For a plain MLP with no such layers it has no visible effect yet, but it's good practice to call consistently.
